The present study raises important questions for future research - this is not a weakness, since one study cannot answer all questions, but points to the importance of the questions raised by this study and the value of additional future research in the area.

claims.claim: Attentional capture by an irrelevant salient distractor is attenuated when the distractor appears more frequently in one location.
claims.source: Attentional capture by an irrelevant salient distractor is attenuated when the distractor appears more frequently in one location, suggesting learned suppression of that location.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that motivates the study.

claims.claim: It remains unclear whether suppression is proactive (before attention is directed) or reactive (after attention is allocated).
claims.source: However, it remains unclear whether suppression is proactive (before attention is directed) or reactive (after attention is allocated).
claims.evidence: This is explicitly stated as the research question in the abstract.

claims.claim: Participants searched for a shape singleton while ignoring a color singleton distractor at a high-probability location in an EEG experiment.
claims.source: In an EEG experiment, participants searched for a shape singleton while ignoring a color singleton distractor at a high-probability location.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claims.claim: Search was more efficient when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location.
claims.source: Behaviorally, search was more efficient when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location.
claims.evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment reported in the abstract.

claims.claim: Inverted encoding analysis of EEG data showed tuning profiles that decayed during memory maintenance but were revived by the placeholder display.
claims.source: Inverted encoding analysis of EEG data showed tuning profiles that decayed during memory maintenance but were revived by the placeholder display.
claims.evidence: This describes a key neural finding from the EEG analysis.

claims.claim: Tuning was most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location, suggesting initial spatial selection followed by suppression.
claims.source: Notably, tuning was most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location, suggesting initial spatial selection followed by suppression.
claims.evidence: This is the main finding from the tuning profile analysis.

claims.claim: Learned distractor suppression is a reactive process.
claims.source: These findings suggest that learned distractor suppression is a reactive process, providing new insights into learned spatial distractor suppression mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claims.claim: Visual input is highly repetitive and structured, making it possible to predict what information will appear next based on current sensory input.
claims.source: Recent studies have demonstrated that attentional selection can be so efficient because visual input is highly repetitive and structured, which makes it possible to predict what information will appear next based on the current sensory input (Friston, 2009; Kok et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Extracting regularities from the environment (statistical learning) occurs effortlessly across trials and operates largely outside conscious awareness.
claims.source: Extracting these regularities from the environment, often called statistical learning (Chun and Jiang, 1999; Frost et al., 2015), occurs effortlessly across trials, operates largely outside the realm of conscious awareness, and is not contingent on explicit knowledge of the regularity (Gao and Theeuwes, 2022; Goujon et al., 2015; Turk-Browne et al., 2005; but see Vicente-Conesa et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Statistical learning plays a crucial role in attentional selection in addition to top-down and bottom-up control processes.
claims.source: In addition to top-down and bottom-up control processes (Corbetta and Shulman, 2002; Desimone and Duncan, 1995; Theeuwes, 2010), statistical learning plays a crucial role in attentional selection (Awh et al., 2012; Failing and Theeuwes, 2018; Theeuwes et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: According to the tripartite model of attention, the interaction between top-down, bottom-up, and selection history jointly determines the weights in a spatial priority map.
claims.source: According to the tripartite model of attention (Awh et al., 2012; Theeuwes, 2019; Theeuwes et al., 2022; Theeuwes, 2025), the interaction between top-down, bottom-up, and selection history, a category which encompasses statistical learning as well as other history-based effects, jointly determines the weights in a spatial priority map, which determines, in a winner-take-all fashion, which object is selected (Chelazzi et al., 2019; Zelinsky and Bisley, 2015).
claims.evidence: This describes a theoretical model supported by citations.

claims.claim: Observers can learn which location is most likely to contain the target.
claims.source: Previous studies have demonstrated that observers can learn which location is most likely to contain the target. Geng and Behrmann, 2005, showed that targets presented in high-probability locations (HPL) are detected faster than those in low-probability locations (LPL) (see also Ferrante et al., 2018; Jiang et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Spatial enhancement occurs for the location with the highest likelihood of containing the target before display presentation.
claims.source: Crucially, the probe task showed spatial enhancement for the location with the highest likelihood of containing the target. Based on these findings, it was argued that the amplification of weights within the spatial priority map, driven by statistical learning, takes place preemptively, before the actual display presentation, implying that priority was changed prior to the allocation of attention.
claims.evidence: This is based on findings from Huang et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A 'ping' technique can reveal hidden neural representations within networks of altered synaptic weights.
claims.source: This technique pushes a wave of activity, often via presentation of a high-contrast stimulus, through the visual system to reveal hidden neural representations within networks of altered synaptic weights.
claims.evidence: This describes the ping technique used in working memory research.

claims.claim: Duncan et al., 2023, demonstrated reliable decoding of the high-probability target location in the evoked EEG signal when a visual ping occurred during the interval preceding the presentation of the search display.
claims.source: Duncan et al., 2023, demonstrated that, following the acquisition of a learned priority for a specific spatial location, there was reliable decoding of the high-probability target location in the evoked EEG signal when a visual ping occurred during the interval preceding the presentation of the search display.
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from Duncan et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Distractor interference is reduced when distractors appear at a high-probability distractor location compared to other locations.
claims.source: Employing a modified version of the additional singleton paradigm, where the color singleton distractor appeared with a higher probability at a specific location relative to other locations, Wang and Theeuwes demonstrated that distractor interference was reduced when distractors appeared at this high-probability distractor location as compared to other locations.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Theeuwes studies.

claims.claim: Participants exhibited slower responses when the target was presented at the high-probability distractor location.
claims.source: Furthermore, participants exhibited slower responses when the target was presented at this high-probability distractor location (Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018c also see Ferrante et al., 2018; Goschy et al., 2014), suggesting that the spatial distractor imbalance resulted in learned suppression of the high-probability distractor location (Failing and Theeuwes, 2020; Feldmann-Wüstefeld et al., 2021; Ferrante et al., 2018; Goschy et al., 2014; Huang et al., 2021a; Sauter et al., 2021; Sauter et al., 2021; Allenmark et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022; van Moorselaar and Theeuwes, 2021b; van Moorselaar and Theeuwes, 2022; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018a).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Learned distractor suppression is not restricted to the spatial domain.
claims.source: Such learned distractor suppression is not restricted to the spatial domain, as many studies have demonstrated that distractor interference can be attenuated, or even completely eliminated, through learning about probable distractor features (Gaspelin and Luck, 2018a; Stilwell and Gaspelin, 2021; Stilwell et al., 2022; Vatterott et al., 2018; Failing et al., 2019; Vatterott and Vecera, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to feature-based suppression studies.

claims.claim: Suppression could potentially occur at three distinct time points: before the distractor appears, after distractor onset but before attentional capture, or after attentional capture has occurred.
claims.source: As articulated by Liesefeld et al., 2024, suppression could potentially occur at three distinct time points: first, before the distractor appears, reflecting anticipatory preparation; second, after distractor onset but before attentional capture, indicating rapid early filtering; or third, after attentional capture has occurred.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical framework from Liesefeld et al., 2024.

claims.claim: Responses were slowed when the probe appeared at the high-probability distractor location.
claims.source: Across multiple studies it was found that responses were slowed when the probe appeared at the high-probability distractor location (Huang et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2021b; Kong et al., 2020), even when the probe display was presented prior to the expected onset of the search display (Huang et al., 2023), leading to the conclusion that suppression operates prior to search display onset, and, thus, before the first shift of attention.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claims.claim: Chang et al., 2023, found that probe accuracy was higher at the high-probability distractor location compared to the low-probability location.
claims.source: Contrary to a proactive account, Chang et al., 2023, found that while suppression occurred during the search task, as indicated by reaction times (RTs), probe accuracy was higher at the high-probability distractor location compared to the LPL (see Experiment 2 in Chang et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is a specific finding from Chang et al., 2023.

claims.claim: The high-probability distractor location was initially selected for attentional processing before suppression occurred, supporting a reactive suppression mechanism.
claims.source: This suggests that the HPL was initially selected for attentional processing before suppression occurred, supporting a reactive suppression mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the Chang et al., 2023 findings.

claims.claim: Memory recall deviation was significantly larger at the test phase compared to the training phase.
claims.source: Our findings revealed a significantly larger recall deviation at the test phase compared to the training phase (6.27°±0.95 vs 11.94°±3.55, t(23) = 5.67, p<0.001, d=2.52), indicating that the process of tracking the spatial memory cue was substantially disrupted by the concurrent secondary task in the test phase.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: Overall memory recall performance in the test phase was high, indicating that observers were able to maintain a relatively precise memory representation outside the current focus of attention.
claims.source: Note, that despite being disrupted by the search task, overall memory recall performance in the test phase was nevertheless high, indicating that observers were able to maintain a relatively precise memory representation outside the current focus of attention.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the memory performance data.

claims.claim: Participants exhibited faster responses when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location compared to the low-probability location.
claims.source: The planned paired t-test revealed that participants exhibited faster (t(23) = 10.14, p<0.001, d=0.43) and more accurate (t(23) = 5.19, p<0.001, d=0.71) responses when the distractor appeared at the HPL (MRT = 965 ms, MACC = 92.2%) compared to the LPL (MRT = 1017 ms, MACC = 89.5%), showing a clear effect of statistically learned distractor suppression and replicating previous findings (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: Participants exhibited more accurate responses when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location compared to the low-probability location.
claims.source: The planned paired t-test revealed that participants exhibited faster (t(23) = 10.14, p<0.001, d=0.43) and more accurate (t(23) = 5.19, p<0.001, d=0.71) responses when the distractor appeared at the HPL (MRT = 965 ms, MACC = 92.2%) compared to the LPL (MRT = 1017 ms, MACC = 89.5%), showing a clear effect of statistically learned distractor suppression and replicating previous findings (Ferrante et al., 2018; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: There was a substantial delay in participants' responses when the target was presented at the high-probability location as opposed to the low-probability location.
claims.source: Further confirming the spatial component of suppression, a planned paired t-test on RTs for target location (collapsed across distractor-absent and distractor-present trials) demonstrated a substantial delay in participants' responses when the target was presented at the HPL (M=1018 ms), as opposed to the LPL (M=958 ms, t(23) = 5.45, p<0.001, d=0.48).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claims.claim: Learned suppression scaled with the relative distance to the high-probability location.
claims.source: To further characterize whether the learned suppression scaled with the relative distance to the HPL, we assigned the low-probability trials into one of four distance groups depending on the relative distance between the distractor and the HPL.
claims.evidence: This is tested through a distance-based analysis of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: A significant main effect of distance was found in the analysis of reaction times.
claims.source: A significant main effect was found in the analysis of RTs (F(2.22, 51.06)= 3.87, p = 0.023, ηp2 = 0.14).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the distance analysis.

claims.claim: Responses in the dist-1 condition were faster than those in the dist-2 condition.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 2C, responses in the dist-1 condition (Mdist_1=989 ms) were faster than those in the dist-2 condition (Mdist_2=1034 ms, t(23) = 3.96, p=0.003, d=0.36), and marginally faster than those in the dist-3 condition (Mdist_3=1024 ms, t(23) = 2.83, p=0.058, d=0.28) and dist-4 condition (Mdist_4=1033 ms, t(23) = 2.75, p=0.069, d=0.33).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Mean accuracy analyses showed a main effect of distance.
claims.source: Mean accuracy analyses mimicked these findings (see Figure 2D), showing a main effect of Distance (F(2.13, 49)= 4.20, p = 0.019, ηp2 = 0.15).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Performance in the dist-1 condition was more accurate than in the dist-2 condition.
claims.source: Performance in the dist-1 condition (Mdist_1=92.6%) was more accurate than in the dist-2 condition (Mdist_2=88.1%, t(23) = 4.24, p=0.002, d=0.86), and in the dist-3 condition (Mdist_3=88.7%, t(23) = 2.97, p=0.041, d=0.75), and marginally more accurate than in the dist-4 condition (Mdist_4=87.7%, t(23) = 2.87, p=0.052, d=0.73).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the distance analysis.

claims.claim: Trials with repeated distractor locations were 41 ms faster compared to trials with non-repeated distractor locations.
claims.source: Consistent with previous research, we found that trials with repeated distractor locations were 41 ms faster (t(23) = 6.32, p<0.001, d=0.33) and 2.1% more accurate (t(23) = 4.21, p<0.001, d=0.86) compared to trials with non-repeated distractor locations.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the intertrial effects analysis.

claims.claim: Excluding trials with repeated distractor locations did not alter the main findings related to distractor regularity or the distance effect.
claims.source: Importantly, excluding trials with repeated distractor locations did not alter the main findings related to distractor regularity or the distance effect, suggesting that intertrial effects alone cannot fully account for the learned suppression effects induced by spatial distractor imbalances.
claims.evidence: This is a control analysis result.

claims.claim: Both evoked and total alpha power generated reliable CTFs in response to memory display onset.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work (Foster et al., 2016; Foster et al., 2017; van Moorselaar et al., 2018), both evoked and total alpha power generated reliable CTFs in response to memory display onset (p<0.05), with evoked power returning to baseline relatively early in the delayed period (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), whereas total alpha power enabled reliable CTF reconstruction throughout the entire delay period (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the localizer data analysis shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The evoked CTFs were distinctly revived upon the presentation of the placeholder display.
claims.source: Critically, as depicted in Figure 3B, the evoked CTFs were distinctly revived upon the presentation of the placeholder display (p<0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the localizer data analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Individual CTF profiles following the memory cue onset were finely tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations with comparable response strengths.
claims.source: (C) illustrates that individual CTF profiles, following the memory cue onset, were finely tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations with comparable response strengths.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Individual CTF profiles tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations were revived by the placeholder to a similar extent.
claims.source: (D) shows that individual CTF profiles tuned to each of the eight spatial cue locations were revived by the placeholder to a similar extent, although the effect was somewhat obscured in the fourth row of the panel.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The data from the training set did not exhibit a spatial bias from the outset.
claims.source: These analyses confirm that the data from the training set did not exhibit a spatial bias from the outset and can thus serve as a neutral independent dataset to investigate how distractor learning in the test phase would, if at all, modulate attentional tuning across all display locations.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the localizer data analysis.

claims.claim: The averaged tuning profiles resulting from cross-session encoding mimicked the pattern of the localizer.
claims.source: As depicted in Figure 4, the averaged tuning profiles resulting from this cross-session encoding procedure mimicked the pattern of the localizer, indicating that the training data could be used to successfully track the memoranda during the test phase with an intermediate search task.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cross-session encoding analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Total power no longer tracked the memorized position throughout the entire delay interval but instead returned to baseline prior to placeholder onset.
claims.source: One main difference was observed on total power, such that it no longer tracked the memorized position throughout the entire delay interval but instead returned to baseline prior to placeholder onset (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cross-session encoding analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Spatial information was revived by the placeholder, an effect that was selective to evoked power.
claims.source: Critically, this information was again revived by the placeholder, an effect that was selective to evoked power (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a result from the cross-session encoding analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The prospect of a secondary task during the memory maintenance interval shifted the memory from an activity-driven into an activity-silent state.
claims.source: Together, these findings are consistent with a model wherein the prospect of a secondary task during the memory maintenance interval shifted the memory from an activity-driven into an activity-silent state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-session encoding results.

claims.claim: Upon placeholder onset, the instantiated neutral input probed the system's underlying activity-silent state, revealing its spatially tuned priority weights.
claims.source: Upon placeholder onset, the instantiated neutral input probed the system's underlying activity-silent state, revealing its spatially tuned priority weights (analogous to the pinging procedure).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-session encoding results.

claims.claim: The revival of the CTF by the placeholder display indicates that the hidden attentional priority map can still be reactivated despite the introduction of a secondary search task.
claims.source: The revival of the CTF by the placeholder display indicates that the hidden attentional priority map, which tracks the location of the memory cue, can still be reactivated despite the introduction of a secondary search task.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the cross-session encoding results.

claims.claim: During the memory encoding period and the maintenance period prior to placeholder onset, both the HPL-matched and LPL-matched CTFs are robust and highly overlap.
claims.source: First, during the memory encoding period immediately following memory cue onset and the maintenance period prior to placeholder onset, both the HPL-matched and LPL-matched CTFs are robust (p<0.05) and highly overlap, indicating that, at this stage, the memory representation is unaffected by the spatial regularity of the distractor location.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Upon placeholder onset, reliable CTF reconstruction is observed in both HPL-matched and LPL-matched conditions, with the HPL-matched CTFs becoming numerically more pronounced than the LPL-matched CTFs.
claims.source: Second, upon placeholder onset, reliable CTF reconstruction is observed in both conditions (p<0.05), with the HPL-matched CTFs becoming numerically more pronounced than the LPL-matched CTFs.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Memory cue locations overlapping with high-probability distractor locations were more strongly selected compared to those overlapping with low-probability locations.
claims.source: Although this conditional difference was not statistically significant, the observed pattern suggests that memory cue locations overlapping with high-probability distractor locations were more strongly selected compared to those overlapping with LPL.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the results shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The resulting CTF profiles varied depending on their distances to the high-probability distractor location.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 5B, in line with a spatial gradient, the resulting CTF profiles varied depending on their distances to the high-probability distractor location.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the distance-based analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: A cluster-based permutation test identified a reliable gradient centered around the high-probability location following placeholder onset.
claims.source: A cluster-based permutation test conducted on the slopes of the regression model identified a reliable gradient (p<0.05) centered around the HPL following placeholder onset.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the distance-based analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The gradient reflected an increase of spatial selectivity centered at the high-probability distractor location rather than an attenuation.
claims.source: Critically, this gradient reflected an increase of spatial selectivity centered at the high-probability distractor location rather than an attenuation, suggesting that immediately following placeholder onset the to-be-suppressed location was at least transiently attended before being suppressed during visual search in the subsequent display.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the gradient analysis results.

claims.claim: At the behavioral level, responses were faster when the distractor occurred at the high-probability location, but slower when the target occurred at this location.
claims.source: At the behavioral level, responses were faster when the distractor occurred at the HPL, but slower when the target occurred at this location, indicative of generic spatial suppression, an effect that was characterized by a discernible spatial gradient centered at the high-probability distractor location.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the behavioral findings in the Discussion.

claims.claim: At the neural level, there was no evidence that spatial suppression attenuated processing at the high-probability distractor location in anticipation of a new search episode.
claims.source: Yet, critically, at the neural level, there was no evidence that this spatial suppression attenuated processing at the high-probability distractor location in anticipation of a new search episode.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the neural findings in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The revival of the CTF profile within the alpha-band showed the largest tuning at the learned suppressed location.
claims.source: Instead of a model that assumes that the HPL was proactively suppressed, the revival of the CTF profile within the alpha-band showed the largest tuning at the learned suppressed location.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the key neural finding in the Discussion.

claims.claim: The modulation of the memory-tuned CTF profile was characterized by a spatial gradient that was centered over the high-probability location.
claims.source: Moreover, the modulation of the memory-tuned CTF profile was characterized by a spatial gradient that was centered over the HPL.
claims.evidence: This summarizes the gradient finding in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Suppression is engaged following the initial selection of a location, indicating a tendency toward a reactive suppression mechanism.
claims.source: These findings suggest that suppression is engaged following the initial selection of a location, indicating a tendency toward a reactive suppression mechanism within the specific context of our study.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claims.claim: Suppression may occur after attentional enhancement rather than being proactively implemented.
claims.source: This implies that suppression may occur after attentional enhancement rather than being proactively implemented.
claims.evidence: This is an implication of the main conclusion.

claims.claim: Studies investigating the preparatory bias in response to distractor regularities largely failed to find evidence in support of active preparatory inhibition as indexed via increased alpha power contralateral to the high-probability distractor location.
claims.source: Studies investigating the preparatory bias in response to distractor regularities largely examined topographical modulations of alpha power, given its functional link to reduced cortical excitability. These studies, however, failed to find evidence in support of active preparatory inhibition as indexed via increased alpha power contralateral to the high-probability distractor location (van Moorselaar et al., 2021a; van Moorselaar et al., 2020a; van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2019; but see Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The absence of anticipatory tuning toward the to-be-suppressed location has given rise to the idea that distractor learning operates by changing synaptic efficiency within these regions.
claims.source: This absence of anticipatory tuning toward the to-be-suppressed location has given rise to the idea that distractor learning operates by changing synaptic efficiency within these regions (van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Moorselaar and Slagter, 2020b.

claims.claim: A recent study using rapid invisible frequency tagging demonstrated reduced neural excitability at the high-probability distractor location in the absence of any alpha-band modulations.
claims.source: Consistent with this, a recent study using rapid invisible frequency tagging demonstrated reduced neural excitability at the high-probability distractor location in the absence of any alpha-band modulations (Ferrante et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ferrante et al., 2023.

claims.claim: The revived CTFs were characterized by a spatial gradient centered over the high-probability location, with tuning being most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location.
claims.source: Interestingly, rather than being suppressed, the revived CTFs were characterized by a spatial gradient centered over the HPL, with tuning being most pronounced at the to-be-suppressed location.
claims.evidence: This is a key finding from the study.

claims.claim: The putative priority map, initially tuned by maintaining a spatial location in working memory, was reconfigured by statistical regularities across search displays to align with the imminent search.
claims.source: Together, this suggests that the putative priority map, initially tuned by maintaining a spatial location in WM, was reconfigured by statistical regularities across search displays to align with the imminent search.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: If one assumes that the evoked response elicited by placeholder displays ping the landscape of the priority map, the observed gradient clearly argues against proactive suppression.
claims.source: If one assumes that the evoked response elicited by placeholder displays ping the landscape of this priority map (Duncan et al., 2023), the observed gradient in our study clearly argues against proactive suppression.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of the pinging technique.

claims.claim: A recent behavioral study observed a similar pattern of results showing initial enhancement at the high-probability distractor location before suppression.
claims.source: Although this result is based on an exploratory analysis and should therefore be interpreted with caution, it is noteworthy that a recent behavioral study observed a similar pattern of results (Chang et al., 2023). In a modified version of the capture-probe paradigm, where the probe display onset was not preceded by a placeholder display, participants discriminated the orientation of a tilted bar presented at one of the search locations, revealing initial enhancement at the high-probability distractor location before suppression.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Memory performance (recall) did not vary as a function of the cue's distance from the high-probability location.
claims.source: Memory performance (recall) did not vary as a function of the cue's distance from the HPL (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), whereas the revived CTFs did, indicating that these changes likely reflect contributions from both tasks.
claims.evidence: This is a result shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Distractor learning typically occurs without conscious awareness.
claims.source: Additionally, distractor learning typically occurs without conscious awareness (Gao and Theeuwes, 2022; Wang and Theeuwes, 2018b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The current results clearly argue against a model wherein statistical learning operates by downregulating weights at the to-be-suppressed location.
claims.source: Irrespective however, the current results clearly argue against a model wherein statistical learning operates by downregulating weights at the to-be-suppressed location.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claims.claim: Proactive and reactive suppression processes may not be mutually exclusive and may often contribute concurrently to observed attentional effects.
claims.source: While many studies, including the current one, have attempted to dissociate between proactive and reactive suppression mechanisms, it is plausible that these processes are not mutually exclusive and may often contribute concurrently to observed attentional effects.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical consideration in the Discussion.

claims.claim: A study by Wang et al., 2019, showed that fewer saccades landed at the suppressed location than any other location, consistent with less proactive oculomotor activity at the suppressed location.
claims.source: A study by Wang et al., 2019, showed that fewer saccades landed at the suppressed location than any other location, consistent with the notion that there was less proactive oculomotor activity at the suppressed location resulting in fewer saccades to that location.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: There was evidence for faster disengagement from the high-probability distractor location than the low-probability distractor location, suggesting a reactive mechanism.
claims.source: Critically however, there was also evidence for faster disengagement from the high-probability distractor location than the low-probability distractor location, suggesting the operation of a reactive mechanism where suppression is followed by rapid oculomotor disengagement (Sauter et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sauter et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Visual pings can effectively unveil spatial memories hidden from the ongoing EEG signal.
claims.source: A novel aspect of the current study is that visual pings, here in the shape of a neutral placeholder display, can effectively unveil spatial memories hidden from the ongoing EEG signal.
claims.evidence: This is a key methodological contribution of the study.

claims.claim: The otherwise invisible attentional priority map induced by a spatial imbalance of target probability across trials could be revealed by the 'pinging' technique in conjunction with multivariate pattern analysis and EEG.
claims.source: Recently, we demonstrated that the otherwise, invisible attentional priority map induced by a spatial imbalance of target probability across trials could also be revealed by the 'pinging' technique in conjunction with multivariate pattern analysis and EEG (Duncan et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duncan et al., 2023.

claims.claim: Early ERP components are enhanced in response to visual stimulation at memorized locations.
claims.source: However, while it is well established that early ERP components are enhanced in response to visual stimulation at memorized locations (Awh et al., 2000), to date the pinging technique has exclusively been used to reveal feature-specific information within working memory (Wolff et al., 2015; Wolff et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

results.result: Memory recall performance was disrupted but remained relatively precise when a secondary search task was introduced during the maintenance interval. Memory recall deviation increased significantly from training (6.27°) to test phase (11.94°), but overall performance remained high.
results.evaluation: Claims C23 and C24 are supported by statistical evidence (t(23)=5.67, p<0.001, d=2.52) showing significant disruption, while also demonstrating that participants maintained relatively precise spatial memory representations despite the dual-task demands. The data directly support both the disruption and the maintenance of functional memory performance.

results.result: Behavioral evidence demonstrates learned distractor suppression at the high-probability location. Participants showed faster and more accurate responses when distractors appeared at the HPL compared to LPL, slower responses when targets appeared at the HPL, and a spatial gradient of suppression that scaled with distance from the HPL.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C34 provide converging behavioral evidence with appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, repeated measures ANOVA) and significant p-values. The distance gradient analysis (C28-C32) and control for intertrial effects (C33-C34) strengthen the conclusion. Effect sizes are reported and the pattern replicates previous findings, supporting the existence of learned spatial suppression.

results.result: The localizer phase (training) established that spatial memory representations can be reliably tracked using alpha-band CTFs and revived by placeholder displays. Both evoked and total alpha power generated reliable CTFs without spatial bias across the eight locations.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39 are supported by statistical evidence (p<0.05) and visual data from Figures 3A-D. The analysis confirms no pre-existing spatial bias and establishes the validity of using the training data as an independent dataset for cross-session encoding. This provides the methodological foundation for the main experimental findings.

results.result: Cross-session encoding revealed that spatial memory shifted from activity-driven to activity-silent states during dual-task conditions. Total power no longer tracked memory throughout the delay, but evoked power showed revival of spatial information upon placeholder onset, suggesting the placeholder 'pinged' the hidden priority map.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 are supported by the cross-session IEM analysis shown in Figure 4. The dissociation between total and evoked power provides evidence for activity-silent memory states under dual-task conditions. However, the interpretation relies on assumptions about the pinging mechanism that remain debated in the field (acknowledged in C74-C75).

results.result: Neural evidence shows enhanced rather than suppressed tuning at the high-probability distractor location following placeholder onset. CTFs revealed a spatial gradient centered on the HPL with the strongest tuning at the to-be-suppressed location, suggesting initial attentional selection before suppression.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 present the key neural finding, but C48 explicitly notes the conditional difference was not statistically significant. While C50 reports a significant gradient (p<0.05), the authors acknowledge this is exploratory (C64) and should be interpreted with caution. The interpretation of enhanced tuning as evidence for reactive suppression is plausible but requires additional validation given the exploratory nature and lack of direct statistical comparison between HPL and LPL conditions.

results.result: The study concludes that learned distractor suppression operates reactively rather than proactively. Neural evidence shows no anticipatory attenuation at the HPL; instead, the location is initially attended (enhanced tuning) before suppression occurs, arguing against proactive downregulation of weights in the priority map.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 and C61-C67 present the main theoretical conclusion, but this interpretation faces several challenges: (1) the key neural comparison (C48) was not statistically significant; (2) the gradient analysis (C50-C51) is acknowledged as exploratory; (3) alternative explanations are discussed but not fully ruled out (memory representation changes, anticipatory distractor tuning); (4) the authors acknowledge proactive and reactive mechanisms may not be mutually exclusive (C68). While the pattern is suggestive, the evidence is insufficient to definitively establish reactive over proactive mechanisms.

results.result: Memory recall performance did not vary with distance from the HPL, while revived CTFs did, suggesting CTF modulations reflect contributions from both memory and search tasks. Distractor learning occurs without conscious awareness.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, providing evidence that CTF modulations are not simply due to memory performance changes. Claim C66 is supported by citations to previous research. Together, these address potential alternative explanations for the neural findings.

results.result: The study demonstrates that visual pings (placeholder displays) can reveal hidden spatial memory representations in EEG. This extends the pinging technique from feature-based to spatial working memory, showing that spatial representations can be reconstructed and used to probe attentional priority maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C81 describe a methodological contribution supported by the data in Figures 3-5. The dissociation between training (C76) and test phases (C77) demonstrates the technique's sensitivity. While debate exists about ping mechanisms (C74-C75), the empirical demonstration that spatial memories can be revived and reconstructed is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The study used a predetermined sample size of 24 participants based on previous EEG studies, with three participants replaced to maintain data quality. The study received ethical approval and followed Helsinki Declaration guidelines.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 describe methodological and ethical procedures that are clearly documented. The sample size justification is based on precedent from similar studies, and the replacement criteria are explicitly stated. These are standard practices appropriately reported.

results.result: The introduction establishes the theoretical background on statistical learning, attentional selection, and the debate between proactive versus reactive suppression mechanisms. Prior work shows conflicting evidence, with some studies supporting proactive suppression and others suggesting reactive mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C22 accurately summarize the relevant literature and theoretical framework. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization of the debate (proactive vs. reactive suppression) is well-documented. This provides proper context for the current study's research question (C2).

results.result: Previous studies using alpha-band power failed to find evidence for proactive inhibition at high-probability distractor locations, leading to theories about synaptic efficiency changes. Some studies show mixed evidence with both proactive (fewer saccades) and reactive (faster disengagement) components.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 and C69-C70 accurately cite relevant prior work that failed to find proactive suppression signatures in alpha power, while C64 cites behavioral work consistent with the current findings. These claims appropriately contextualize the current study's contribution and acknowledge complexity in the literature.

results.result: The authors acknowledge important limitations and alternative interpretations: proactive and reactive mechanisms may coexist, debate exists about ping mechanisms, and the specific mechanism underlying activity-silent states remains uncertain.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C74-C75, and C78 demonstrate appropriate scientific caution by acknowledging theoretical debates, mechanistic uncertainties, and the possibility that their dichotomous framing (proactive vs. reactive) may be oversimplified. This strengthens rather than weakens the paper by showing awareness of limitations.

results.result: Behavioral results showed that search was more efficient (faster and more accurate responses) when the distractor appeared at the high-probability location (HPL) compared to the low-probability location (LPL), and slower when the target appeared at the HPL. This suppression effect exhibited a spatial gradient centered at the HPL, with performance scaling by distance from the HPL.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly acknowledged the behavioral findings as supporting prior literature on distractor suppression. Reviewer 2 stated 'the study also provides behavioral results supporting prior literature on distractor suppression at high-probability locations,' and Reviewer 3 noted 'the authors have also conducted additional behavioral analyses to examine the relationship between memory and search.' No concerns were raised about these behavioral effects.

results.result: EEG inverted encoding analysis revealed that tuning profiles decayed during memory maintenance but were revived by the placeholder display. Critically, following placeholder onset, tuning was most pronounced at the high-probability distractor location and exhibited a spatial gradient centered over that location, reflecting increased spatial selectivity rather than attenuation at the to-be-suppressed location.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these neural findings as the core contribution of the study. Reviewer 1 stated 'the authors found evidence that despite learning to suppress the high probability distractor location, the suppression was reactive, not proactive in nature,' and Reviewer 3 noted 'the main finding is that neural responses to the probe indicate that the high probability location is attended, rather than suppressed, prior to the search display onset.' The editor described the results as 'compelling,' though 'open to multiple interpretations.'

results.result: The study concludes that learned distractor suppression is a reactive process, where suppression is engaged following initial spatial selection of the high-probability location, rather than being proactively implemented before attention is directed. This argues against models wherein statistical learning operates by downregulating weights at the to-be-suppressed location in anticipation of search.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the findings, they noted openness to alternative interpretations. The editor stated the results are 'compelling, although they are open to multiple interpretations.' Reviewer 2 noted 'while, to some degree, the results may still remain open to alternative explanations, the study, in its current form, presents an interesting paradigm and promising findings.' Reviewers accepted the authors' tempering of claims and discussion of alternative mechanisms, indicating the conclusion is plausible but not definitively established.

results.result: Cross-session encoding showed that training data could successfully track memoranda during the test phase, but total power no longer tracked the memorized position throughout the delay interval, returning to baseline before placeholder onset. Spatial information was revived by the placeholder in evoked power, suggesting memory shifted to an activity-silent state during dual-task conditions. This demonstrates that visual pings can unveil spatial memories hidden from ongoing EEG signal.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the methodological innovation. Reviewer 3 stated 'this was a creative approach to a difficult and important question about attention. The use of this "pinging" method to assess the attentional priority map has a lot of potential value.' Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'clarified and further discussed several methodological aspects' and that 'the use of a secondary task and EEG/IEM to provide a direct assessment of hidden priority maps in anticipation of a distractor is, in principle, a clever approach.' No concerns were raised about these methodological findings.

results.result: Memory recall deviation was significantly larger at the test phase compared to training phase, indicating disruption by the concurrent search task. However, overall memory performance remained high, and memory recall did not vary as a function of distance from the HPL, whereas revived CTFs did, suggesting the neural changes reflect contributions from both tasks.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly noted 'the authors have also conducted additional behavioral analyses to examine the relationship between memory and search,' indicating acceptance of these control analyses. Reviewer 2 acknowledged the authors addressed concerns about 'alternative explanations due to the dual-task design,' suggesting these memory performance analyses were satisfactory. No reviewer challenged these findings.

results.result: Intertrial effects were observed (trials with repeated distractor locations were faster and more accurate), but excluding these trials did not alter the main findings related to distractor regularity or distance effects, suggesting intertrial effects alone cannot fully account for learned suppression effects.
results.evaluation: This control analysis was not specifically discussed by reviewers, but Reviewer 2's statement that 'the authors have clarified and further discussed several methodological aspects, limitations, and alternative interpretations' and that prior weaknesses were 'largely addressed' suggests acceptance of such control analyses. No concerns were raised about confounding intertrial effects.

results.result: The study used a predetermined sample size of 24 participants in an EEG experiment where participants searched for a shape singleton while ignoring a color singleton distractor at a high-probability location. Three participants were replaced to ensure data quality. The study received ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the experimental design, sample size, or ethical procedures. Reviewer 1 noted 'the manuscript is well-written, clear, and concise (especially given the complexities of the method and analyses)' and 'the presentation of the logic and results is clear and relatively easy to digest,' implicitly accepting the methodological approach.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations support the methodological and ethical procedures (C84-C86). OpenEval explicitly notes these are standard practices appropriately reported, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted them without raising concerns about experimental design or sample size.

Both strongly support the behavioral findings on distractor suppression (C25-C32). OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence with appropriate statistics and effect sizes, while peer reviewers explicitly acknowledged these results as supporting prior literature with no concerns raised.

Both support the dual-task memory findings (C23-C24). OpenEval notes statistical evidence for both disruption and maintained functional performance, while peer reviewers accepted the behavioral analyses examining memory-search relationships and alternative explanations due to dual-task design.

Both support the methodological innovation of the pinging technique (C71-C81). OpenEval describes it as a well-supported methodological contribution with demonstrated sensitivity, while peer reviewers praised it as creative and clever with 'a lot of potential value.'

Both address the core neural findings (C46-C51) but with different emphases. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to non-significant conditional difference (C48) and exploratory nature, while peer reviewers rated SUPPORTED, accepting these as the main contribution despite acknowledging openness to interpretation.

Both rate the main theoretical conclusion (reactive vs. proactive suppression) as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval cites non-significant comparisons, exploratory analyses, and unresolved alternative explanations. Peer reviewers similarly note results are 'open to multiple interpretations' and 'may still remain open to alternative explanations.'

Both support the cross-session IEM analysis and activity-silent memory findings (C40-C45). OpenEval notes support with caveat about debated ping mechanisms, while peer reviewers praised the methodological approach without raising concerns about these specific claims.

Both support the validation analyses (C35-C36). OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence for no pre-existing bias and methodological foundation, while peer reviewers accepted these as part of the core neural contribution without specific concerns.

Both support the control analysis addressing alternative explanations (C65). OpenEval cites Figure 2 supplement data showing CTF modulations aren't due to memory performance changes, while peer reviewers acknowledged authors addressed alternative explanations satisfactorily.

Both support the intertrial control analysis (C33-C34). OpenEval explicitly notes this strengthens conclusions, while peer reviewers implicitly accepted it as part of methodological aspects that were 'largely addressed.'

OpenEval supports the literature review and theoretical framework (C1-C22), noting appropriate citations and well-documented characterization of the proactive vs. reactive debate. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these background claims.

OpenEval supports the contextualization claims citing prior work on alpha power and behavioral findings (C58-C60, C64, C69-C70). No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addressed these literature contextualization claims.

OpenEval supports the acknowledgment of limitations and theoretical debates (C68, C74-C75, C78), viewing this as appropriate scientific caution. Peer reviewers implicitly accepted these caveats, with one noting the authors 'clarified and further discussed several methodological aspects, limitations, and alternative interpretations.'

Peer reviewers supported claim C4 (experimental design) and C52 (main conclusion about reactive suppression) as part of their evaluation. OpenEval addressed C52 in R6 (rated UNCERTAIN) but did not create a separate result for C4.

Peer reviewers addressed C7 (research question) and C22 (theoretical framework) as part of their UNCERTAIN evaluation of the main conclusion. OpenEval addressed C22 in R10 (literature review, rated SUPPORTED) but did not separately evaluate C7.
